messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Politician
  trauma_type: Life-threatening accident
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Discomfort: Feeling uncomfortable, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong, Rumination: Self-Blame: repeatedly blame myself for what happened, Avoid Driving: Driving or being a passenger in a vehicle
  Threat: Waking Alert: I wake during the night to check whether I am safe, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating
  Memory: Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event
  Negative Appraisals: Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am, Hypervigilance: I have to be on guard all the time, Exposed to Others: I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Gerald Howarth is a 68-year-old married politician of European descent who has spent the better part of four decades in public life, accustomed to scrutiny and the performance of composure. He presented for psychological assessment approximately eight months after a life-threatening road traffic accident that he has struggled, in his own words, to "put behind him the way a man of my experience should be able to."

The accident occurred on a wet November evening when Gerald was being driven home from a late legislative session. His driver, who Gerald later learned had consumed alcohol before the journey, lost control of the vehicle on a highway interchange. The car was struck broadside by a lorry, spun across two lanes, and came to rest against a concrete barrier. Gerald sustained fractured ribs, a collapsed lung, and lacerations to his face and left arm. He was conscious throughout, pinned against the crumpled door, aware of the smell of alcohol emanating from the driver and of the particular silence that descended after the impact — a silence that preceded the sound of approaching sirens by what felt to him like an eternity. He remembers the event not as a continuous sequence but as a series of frozen images: the headlights of the lorry filling the window, the driver's hands leaving the wheel, the angle of the crushed metal against his chest. He has found, in the months since, that when he attempts to recount the accident — to his wife, to colleagues who have asked — he loses the thread somewhere in the middle, the words dissolving before he can reach the end, leaving him staring at whoever is listening with a sentence unfinished.

In the weeks following his discharge from hospital, Gerald noticed that the smell of alcohol — at receptions, at the parliamentary bar, at the dinner table when wine was poured — produced an immediate and overwhelming wave of discomfort that he could not rationalise away. He began declining evening events where drinking was likely, offering scheduling conflicts as the reason. He also stopped travelling by car entirely. This was not a minor inconvenience for a working politician. His constituency is rural, his diary demanding. He began arriving late to votes, missing engagements he had previously considered non-negotiable, and delegating travel to junior staff under the pretence of workload. His chief of staff has quietly noted the change. Gerald is aware that colleagues have begun to talk, and this awareness compounds something he has come to believe with a conviction that surprises even him: that people can look at him now and see what happened, that the accident is somehow visible on him, legible in his face or his bearing. In committee rooms and on the floor of the chamber, he has found concentration increasingly difficult to sustain, his attention drifting mid-debate in ways that would once have been unthinkable.

At night, Gerald wakes repeatedly, often rising to check that the house is locked, that his wife is breathing, that nothing is wrong — unable to articulate what he is checking for, only that the waking feels necessary. Unusual quiet — the absence of traffic, a lull in conversation — produces in him a specific and visceral dread, as though silence itself has become a harbinger. When the memories return, they are accompanied by a physical sensation of pressure across his chest and pain along the left side of his ribcage, the body apparently rehearsing what the mind cannot finish.

What has weighed on Gerald most persistently is a form of self-recrimination he cannot seem to reason his way out of. He dwells repeatedly on the fact that he chose that driver, that he had ignored a prior complaint about the man's reliability, that he had been in a hurry. He has come to believe, with a quiet but immovable certainty, that the accident happened because of the kind of man he is — someone who prioritises efficiency over care, whose judgment cannot be trusted. This belief sits beneath his public life like a fault line.

Gerald sought help only after his wife told him she was frightened — not of him, but for him. What he most fears, sitting in the consulting room, is that speaking about it will confirm what he already suspects about himself. What he most hopes is that it will not.
